content: I specialize in early undergraduate mathematics education, having dedicated my career to it after finishing my Ph.D. in Math in 2009 under the supervision of John Harer. For the past decade, I have taught and supervised Math 105L and 106L, entry-level laboratory calculus courses at Duke. I have edited and created labs for these courses, introducing technological and pedagogical innovations adapted to each year’s students. I have served as a college (pre-major) advisor to dozens of undergraduate students and as major advisor to a few. In 2017, I won Duke’s Advisor of the Year Award, as chosen by the Academic Advising Center based on comments from my advisees. I live in Durham, North Carolina with my partner and young child. My pronouns are he/him/his.

Math 105L: Video Project One of your major bits of work for the semester will be to create a video explaining a mathematical concept, either one from our class, or any other bit of math you find interesting or are curious about. This sheet outlines the project, the timeline for it, its structure, and its assessment.
Organization You will work in groups of four or three (most groups will be three). All students must appear in the video, and all students must do approximately equal work on topic selection and the storyboard/script (see below). Your video can be longish (up to eight minutes) or short (but no less than 2.5 minutes) - the key is to clearly explain a concept!. My suggestion would be to use TikTok. However, you may use any software you like.
Content The video you write, storyboard, and produce will introduce or explain a mathematical concept to a calculus student audience. You may pick a calculus topic or something outside calculus. Some ideas are:
105L Concepts Others What is a Limit? Zeno’s Paradoxes Finding Tangent Lines Fractals Using Log Rules to Solve Equations Tessellations Continuity and Differentiability The Möbius strip and Klein Bottle Using the Product and Quotient Rules Non-Euclidean Geometry The Chain Rule The history of zero Transforming Functions The Abacus What does the slope of a curve mean? The Fibonacci Sequence and the Golden Ratio What concavity tells us about human growth Hotel Infinity Proving the Power Rule You do not have to choose from this list – any mathematical topic you come up with may work! Just check your idea with me!
Your video can be serious or silly. It can be spoken or sung. It can use a whiteboard or paper, or take place outside. It can be about how you understood a concept that started off being really hard, or explain another interesting bit of math.
Structure You will produce two major bits of work for the project: A storyboard and script (click that link to find out what a storyboard is!); and the video itself.
Timeline You will need to meet and research a topic by Monday, Nov 2. On that day, your group should send me an email with your choice of topic and a list of resources you plan to use to learn about it. I will reply within a day or two, either asking for a bit more detail (or more resources), or approving your decision.s The storyboard and script for your video will be due Friday, Nov 13 at 8am. I would be more than happy to meet to discuss your work once in between these dates. It would be a good idea for your group to plan to have such a meeting with me. I will grade and return the storyboard and script to you within a week. I may ask you to make revisions. If so, those will be due Wednesday, Nov 18 Your final video will be presented to the class during Week 15, the week after Thanksgiving. Your group will be assigned a slot to present in, on Monday or Friday of Week 15. Assessment You will need to pass both the storyboard and script assignment and the final video assignment in order to getting a passing grade for this element of the class:
Storyboard Your storyboard must include a slide for each scene of your video, explaining what will be seen and heard.
Script Your script should include all text spoken (or sung!) for each scene. The script must clearly explain the mathematical concept you choose. 50% of the script must pertain directly to the mathematical concept you choose. The script must be mathematically accurate.
Video You will get judged on the audio/visual clarity and quality; group participation (all members must be participating); and matching the script/storyboard.
Suggestions It would be useful for you to watch a few videos that explain math concepts well and in an engaging way. Here are some TikTok channels to get you started. Importantly, however, you cannot copy someone else’s video or idea - as always, the work must be your own.
